full_narrative: Traditional accounts describe large, hair-covered forest dwellers who inhabit high mountain ridges. Known to communicate via wood knocks and vocal whistles, maintaining distance from human settlements.
In Koyukon tradition, solitary hairy giants inhabit the dense taiga along river valleys. They are described as powerful, elusive beings who leave oversized tracks near waterways during salmon runs.
Traditional Haida lore describes the Gogit as wild, hair-covered humans living in the outer coastal timber. They are characterized by reddish hair, wild vocalizations, and nighttime foraging.
Klamath oral history speaks of large, upright creatures dwelling in the Cascade forests. They are noted for rock throwing, tree shaking, and keeping watch over high elevation passes.
Yokuts elders recorded descriptions of hairy giant figures depicted in ancient pictographs (such as the Painted Rock sites). Described as forest protectors who walk bipedally through oak groves.
